chapter.title: When something breaks: describing the leak, not guessing the pipe

cards.body:
Your app just turned into a wall of red text, and your hand is already moving to close the window. Don't close it. That red text is the most useful thing on your screen.

When a house has a leak, you don't tell your contractor "I think it's the joint behind the fridge." You show them the puddle, say when it appeared, and let them find the pipe. **Describe the leak, not your guess about the pipe.**
cards.simpler: Your app just filled up with red text, and you want to close the window. Don't. That red text is the most useful thing on your screen. If your house had a leak, you wouldn't tell the contractor which pipe you think it is. You'd show them the puddle, say when it showed up, and let them find the pipe. **Describe the leak, not your guess about the pipe.**

cards.prompt: Your to-do app worked fine for 3 clicks of "Add". On the 4th click, the screen fills with red text. What do you send Claude?

options.text: "I think the database is broken. Please rewrite it."
The red text, copied in full, plus: "I clicked Add 4 times. On the 4th, the screen went red."

whyNot.a: That's a guess about the pipe, not the leak: Claude might rebuild a part that was working fine.
whyNot.c: That's a feeling, not a report: Claude doesn't know what you did or what you saw.

cards.reteach: Your builder is good at finding pipes, but only if you show them the puddle. The puddle is the error text plus the steps that caused it. Your theory about the cause can wait.

cards.title: The note the computer leaves
cards.body:
An *error message* is a note the computer leaves when something fails. It reads like gibberish because it was written for programmers: usually a file name, a line number and a short complaint. Those details tell the builder exactly which pipe to open. **You don't need to understand it. Copy all of it.**

You'll find it in one of two places. One is the terminal where your app is running. The other is the browser's *console*, a hidden panel you open in Chrome by right-clicking the page, choosing Inspect, then the Console tab.

Then add two plain sentences: what you did, step by step, and what you saw compared with what you expected.
cards.simpler: An error message is a note the computer leaves when something goes wrong. It looks like nonsense because it's meant for programmers. It often names a file, a line and the problem. **You don't need to understand it. Copy all of it.** Look in the terminal, the text window running your app, or in Chrome's Console: right-click the page, pick Inspect, then Console. Then add what you did, and what you saw compared with what you expected.

cards.title: Maya and the blank recipe box
cards.body:
Maya built a recipe saver. She typed "Mum's dal", pressed Save, and the whole page went white. The console said: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map').

She pasted that line into Claude with: "I typed a recipe name and pressed Save. I expected it in the list. The page went blank instead." Claude found that the page tried to show the list before the list existed, and fixed it in one line.

Maya still doesn't know what 'map' means. She didn't need to.
cards.simpler: Maya made a recipe saver. She typed "Mum's dal", pressed Save, and the page went white. The console showed: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map'). **She pasted that line into Claude** with: "I typed a recipe name and pressed Save. I expected it in the list. The page went blank instead." Claude found the page tried to show the list too early, and fixed it in one line. Maya doesn't know what 'map' means. She didn't need to.

cards.prompt: Jonas's quiz app shows no red text anywhere, but after question 3 the score reads "NaN" (computer-speak for "not a number"). Which message gives Claude the best chance?

options.text: "Score shows NaN. Probably bad maths in the scoring file. Rewrite the scoring."
"I answered questions 1 to 3, all correct. After question 3 the score says NaN instead of 3. No error in the terminal or console."

whyNot.a: That's guessing the pipe: Claude may rewrite the scoring when the leak is somewhere else.
whyNot.c: That's a mood, not the steps: "sometimes" gives Claude nothing to repeat.

cards.reteach: With no red text, your steps and what you saw become the whole report. "I did this, I expected that, I got this instead" is enough for the builder to repeat the problem and track it down.

cards.title: "Fixed!" means "I changed something"
cards.body:
You'd think "Fixed!" means fixed. It actually means "I changed something." A contractor who says the leak is sealed still expects you to turn on the tap. **Repeat the exact steps that broke it, and watch.**

Maya saves a recipe again. Then one more, this time with an empty name, just to poke it. If both work, it's fixed.

If it breaks again, don't start over. Paste the new error with "Same steps, new message:" in front. Two or three rounds of this is normal. It doesn't mean you're bad at this.
cards.simpler: "Fixed!" doesn't mean fixed. It means "I changed something." A contractor who seals a leak still expects you to turn on the tap. **Repeat the exact steps that broke it, and watch.** Maya saves another recipe, then one with an empty name. If both work, it's fixed. If it breaks again, don't start over. Paste the new error, starting with "Same steps, new message:". Two or three rounds is normal. It's not a sign you're bad at this.

cards.body: Sam saw "Module not found", remembered a forum post, and told Claude to "reinstall everything." Claude did, twenty minutes went by, and the same message came back. The real problem was a misspelled file name, and the error had said which file. How to spot it: if your message says "I think it's..." but doesn't include the error itself, you're guessing the pipe.
cards.simpler: Sam saw "Module not found", remembered a tip from an online forum, and told Claude to "reinstall everything." Claude did. Twenty minutes later, the same message came back. The real problem was a misspelled file name, and the error had named the file. Here's the warning sign: **if your message says "I think it's..." but leaves out the error, you're guessing the pipe.**

cards.prompt: Why paste the whole error instead of summing it up as "something about a module"?

options.text: The file name and line number in it tell Claude exactly where to look.
Longer messages make Claude try harder.

whyNot.a: That mixes up reading with evidence: Claude understands your words fine, but a summary drops the file and line details.
whyNot.c: That's length, not detail: a long vague message is still vague. The clues are what help.

cards.reteach: The error is like a puddle under one particular pipe: it points to the spot. A summary is like saying "the kitchen's wet somewhere." Hand over the exact text and the builder can go straight to the right place.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
When something breaks, copy the whole error, then add what you did and what you saw, and let Claude find the pipe. When it says "fixed", repeat the steps that broke it before you believe it.

Tomorrow: how to bring back yesterday's working app with one sentence.
cards.simpler: When something breaks, **copy the whole error**. Then add what you did and what you saw, and let Claude find the pipe. When Claude says "fixed", repeat the steps that broke it before you believe it. Tomorrow: how to bring back yesterday's working app with one sentence.

cards.body: Open your app from chapter 1 in Chrome and open the Console (right-click, Inspect, Console). Ask Claude: "Add a button that breaks on purpose so I can practise." Click it, copy the error, and ask for a fix.
cards.simpler: Open your app from chapter 1 in Chrome. Open the Console: right-click the page, choose Inspect, then Console. Ask Claude: "Add a button that breaks on purpose so I can practise." Click the button, **copy the error that appears**, and ask Claude to fix it.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now take a red error screen to a fixed, tested app by handing Claude the message, your steps, and what you saw.
